title: Wearable Panic Detox Booth
oneLiner: A playful health-tech reset that helps obsessive smartwatch and ring checkers turn scary metrics into calmer experiments and shareable boundaries.
targetUser: Smartwatch, smart ring, HRV, sleep-score, and recovery-score users who compulsively check metrics and want a lighter way to regain control.
keyUX: Users pick their panic metric, reveal the checking loop, set a tiny experiment, hide noisy numbers, and generate a funny boundary card for themselves or friends.
requiredUISections: Number hiding and notification boundary controls

externalSignalRefs.source: EMARKETER, "Many consumers call for bigger tech role in daily wellness"
externalSignalRefs.observed: More consumers use smart scales, connected health devices, and daily wellness tech, expanding the data stream people must interpret.

externalSignalRefs.source: Reddit r/AskDocs, "Do wearable devices help people with health anxiety or make it worse?"
externalSignalRefs.observed: Wearables can worsen anxiety, with some users obsessively checking uncertain metrics and symptoms.

stitchPrompt: Design a playful experimental web product called Wearable Panic Detox Booth for smartwatch, smart ring, HRV, sleep-score, and recovery-score users who compulsively check metrics and want a lighter way to regain control. Users choose the metric that scares them, map their checking loop, learn what the signal can and cannot prove, set a tiny real-world experiment, hide noisy numbers for a chosen window, prepare doctor questions when needed, and generate a shareable calm-data boundary card. Include a panic metric selector, checking-loop confession wheel, signal-versus-noise explainer cards, tiny experiment builder, number hiding and notification boundary controls, doctor-question note pad, detox streak booth, and shareable calm-data boundary card. Design direction: use the playful-experimental profile with bright clinic-arcade energy, tactile booth controls, friendly warning labels, expressive but legible data cards, and one obvious panic-to-boundary flow so the concept feels funny and portfolio-worthy without trivializing health anxiety.
